entities.name: Fatimid Caliphate
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Fatimid Caliphate (909–1171 CE) was an Ismaili Shia Islamic caliphate that, at its peak, controlled Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Sicily, the Levant, and the Hejaz (western Arabia including Mecca and Medina). The Fatimids posed the most significant Shia challenge to Sunni Abbasid supremacy in Islamic history and founded Cairo as their capital in 969 CE.

Under the Fatimid caliph al-Muizz, the general Jawhar al-Siqilli conquered Egypt in 969 CE and built Cairo (al-Qahira, 'The Victorious') as a planned capital city. The Fatimids established Al-Azhar mosque and university in Cairo in 970-972 CE, which became one of the world's oldest continually operating universities and remains the foremost institution of Sunni Islamic learning (ironically, after Saladin's conversion of Egypt to Sunni Islam).

Fatimid Cairo became one of the medieval world's most prosperous cities, a hub of Mediterranean and Indian Ocean trade. The Fatimid court sponsored magnificent architecture, arts, and scholarship. The dynasty's Ismaili da'wa (mission) spread Shia Islam from Morocco to Central Asia and India, creating Ismaili communities that persist today. Saladin's 1171 restoration of Sunni rule ended the Fatimid caliphate but not the dynasty's architectural and scholarly legacy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Fatimid Caliphate founded Cairo and Al-Azhar university while creating the most significant Shia counterweight to Sunni Abbasid power, leaving enduring institutions that outlasted the dynasty itself.
